canberra.title: This street sign has been neglected for years, so who’s supposed to fix it?
canberra.snippet: A neglected street sign in Canberra’s CBD has raised questions about who is responsible for maintaining the worn-down signage. The ...
canberra.content:
This CBD street sign has been the subject of years of questions about why it hasn’t been fixed and who is responsible. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

A neglected street sign in Canberra’s CBD has raised questions about who is responsible for maintaining the worn-down signage.

The sign is one of many on Bunda and Genge streets, surrounding the Canberra Centre, that are washed out, with chipped or faded paint.

Originally, the sign provided directions to parking and popular locations around the shopping complex, including Dendy Cinema, but in its current state, it is an unreadable blue-and-white board.

Public concerns about the street sign have been raised online, with many asking why it hasn’t been renovated or taken down.

“It’s like an overused credit card from the 80s,” Reddit user andthegeekshall posted.

“It’s been like that for years. I’m all for some rejuvenation projects in the city, but sometimes things just need a bit of fresh paint or a power wash. Or a replacement in this case,” user Gin_and_T replied.

While many street signs across Canberra are the responsibility of the ACT Government, Minister for City and Government Services Tara Cheyne clarified that, in this case, the sign is the Canberra Centre’s responsibility.

“I’ve seen it come up multiple times on social media and I’ve definitely checked who is responsible for them,” Ms Cheyne said.

“We do have a lot of signs around the city that reflect the time that they were installed. Where our focus has been, and where the budget commitment was a few years ago, has been on replacing the signs at the entrances to our city.

“That’s where people will have seen major sign renewal.

“We want Canberra to feel like a welcoming place as soon as you cross the border, and so certainly down south, but especially on the Barton Highway, the approaches there, all of those signs have been progressively renewed, especially this year.”

The sign on Genge Street doesn’t look too flash either. Photos: Jarryd Rowley.

Ms Cheyne confirmed there had been discussion between the ACT Government and the Canberra Centre about the sign but reinforced it is ultimately up to the centre to fix.

“[The Canberra Centre] may have some plans for the sign that we’re not aware of,” she said.

“Perhaps they’re in the market for replacing that sign, but I don’t think the government should be intervening where a major company has the resources to give it an uplift.

“I think the community has made it clear that they think the signs need work, but it is their responsibility.”

Ms Cheyne explained that while new signage doesn’t require a development application, updating and cleaning street signs isn’t cheap.

“It was several hundred thousand dollars for the signs on the Barton Highway approach,” she said.

“Suburban street signs in Canberra are made and replaced by this team in-house, which is a great capability for us to have.

“For some of our smaller roads projects, where we might need to renew a give way sign or repaint some lines on the ground, that team certainly exists and does a great job.

“It’s our bigger projects, the bigger signs, where we don’t necessarily have that sitting in storage. That’s where we’ve needed to go out of our way.”

Region has contacted the Canberra Centre for comment.

canberra.title: Politicians blast Qantas over its ‘un-Australian’ decision to sack 850 workers
canberra.snippet: Federal parliamentarians have lined up to condemn Qantas’s decision to slash 850 Australian jobs, send roles offshore to India, and hand ...
canberra.content:
Qantas is sacking 850 local employees as jobs head offshore and to AI. Photo: Qantas.

Federal parliamentarians have lined up to condemn Qantas’s decision to slash 850 Australian jobs, send roles offshore to India, and hand over admin work to artificial intelligence.

Government ministers have expressed their disappointment at the move, while Nationals leader Matt Canavan has bluntly described it as un-Australian.

Qantas reported $1.3 billion in full-year profits in August, but this week announced an outsourcing deal with tech firm Accenture. The 850 local jobs will be gone by mid-2027.

Senator Canavan said on Wednesday (11 November) that it was a “shocking decision” and laid some of the blame on the Federal Government’s economic management.

“I see it as un-Australian, and I think the Australian Government has got to take some action here,” the Nationals leader said.

“They wouldn’t exist – Qantas – without the support of taxpayers and the Australian Government through COVID and other troubles … We need a reset button over Christmas. Jim Chalmers has got to go. He’s been hopeless and failed as a Treasurer.”

Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles said local jobs should be the company’s focus.

“I think it’s a disappointing decision,” he said of the Qantas announcement.

“It’s obviously very disappointing for the more than 800 workers who are involved here.

“What’s really important, obviously now, is that Qantas is working with them, with their representatives, the unions, to make sure that as many are redeployed as possible.

“I mean, we very much understand that advances in technology will play out. But it’s really important that Australian jobs are a focus here.

“And it’s really incumbent now on Qantas to make sure that they are working with those people and redeploying them where they can.”

Transport Minister Catherine King was even sharper in her criticism, describing the Qantas decision as “incredibly disappointing” and a move that could further damage the airline’s reputation.

“This has been a model that Qantas has been using for some time – outsourcing jobs, no longer having them in-house,” Ms King said.

“It’s not the only company that obviously does that, but the scale of it when Qantas does it is substantial.

“We do need AI capabilities here in this country. We need jobs in this country, and I would hope very much so that Qantas reflects on that and what happened last time when it engaged in such a significant outsourcing exercise and the damage it did to its reputation.”

The Coalition government of Scott Morrison handed Qantas $2.7 billion at the height of the COVID pandemic.

It subsequently recorded huge profits.

It was also ordered to pay $120 million in compensation to 1820 ground crew workers it illegally sacked during COVID.

Ms King said Labor would have considered taking an equity stake in the airline if it had been in government during the pandemic.

“I think certainly when it comes to Qantas, that would have been one of the things that we probably, if we had been in government during COVID, put on the table to them as well,” the Transport Minister said.

“Qantas is the Australian carrier. It’s by law required to have 51 per cent Australian ownership, and that continues.

“That’s obviously a benefit to Australia, but a constraint it has on its capital raising.

“But in return for being Australia’s carrier, I think Australians expect it to invest and continue to invest, as it has done in the past, substantially in Australian jobs.”

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said on Tuesday that the decision was ultimately a matter for Qantas, but the Coalition wanted to see more jobs in Australia.

Greens employment spokesperson Barbara Pocock blasted Qantas and the Federal Government.

“Big corporations are hiding behind claims of cost savings while raking in massive profits. It’s a pathetic excuse for slashing jobs,” Senator Pocock said.

“Workers are paying the price while the corporate giants cash in and Labor is doing nothing to protect workers from AI-driven job cuts.

“Where is Labor, the so-called ‘party for workers’? Too busy signing contracts with Accenture.”

A statement from Qantas announcing the sackings said its partnership with Accenture would redesign and simplify how parts of the company’s corporate functions operate.

“Like every airline, Qantas runs on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together,” the statement said.

“Modernising these systems and connecting the data across them is the critical next step to remove complexity, unlock innovation and accelerate the group’s use of AI, with lasting benefits across the business…

“Some of the services they provide will move to Accenture, delivered mostly by its teams in India and some in Australia, and in time be transformed further with automation and AI.”

canberra.title: Boys charged over alleged assaults at Canberra OzTag game
canberra.snippet: Two teenage boys have been charged after they allegedly assaulted a number of people during a brawl at a sports game in southern Canberra...
canberra.content:
Two 16-year-old boys have been charged with assault over their alleged roles in a brawl. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Two teenage boys have been charged after they allegedly assaulted a number of people during a brawl at a sports game in southern Canberra.

The incident during the ACT OzTag game at the Calwell Playing Fields on 29 October drew attention from the media and concern from the local community.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said a group of teenagers had gone to the game before they allegedly became aggressive towards a teenage player.

When adults attempted to intervene, members of the group allegedly assaulted multiple people.

Afterwards, ACT OzTag released a statement about the “deeply concerning incident”.

“The nature and circumstances of this incident are extremely disturbing,” they said.

“ACT OzTag understands that members of our sporting community were subjected to threatening and harmful conduct, and we regard these allegations with the utmost seriousness.”

The police spokesperson said four teens were identified after an investigation into the alleged brawl.

Two 16-year-old boys, who cannot be identified due to their ages, were charged with assault.

They have already faced the ACT Childrens Court where they were granted bail and will return to court on separate days later in November.

A third 16-year-old boy was issued a caution for breaching a personal protection order.

Anyone who can help police with their investigation can contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or via  Crime Stoppers ACT. Quote 8542132.

canberra.title: Driver crashed into pedestrian, causing life-changing injuries
canberra.snippet: A driver took his hands off the wheel, lost control of his car and crashed into a pedestrian in Canberra, causing life-changing injuries....
canberra.content:
Nathan Deacon, 33, leaving the Magistrates Court after his sentencing on Tuesday. Photo: Albert McKnight.

A driver took his hands off the wheel, lost control of his car and crashed into a pedestrian in Canberra, causing life-changing injuries.

In CCTV that was played to the ACT Magistrates Court, Nathan Deacon’s car could be seen driving down a street in Oaks Estate on the night of 6 February 2026 when a man ran towards the road.

Deacon’s car then swerved, mounted the gutter and hit the man, before driving off. The man was seen getting up and starting to limp away before the footage ended.

He was left with a broken leg, an exposed tibia and heavy bleeding, the court previously heard.

“After he mounted the gutter and hit me, I was abandoned and left there for what I thought was for dead,” the man wrote in a statement that was read to the court on Tuesday (10 November).

“I thought I was going to die.”

He said his injuries were catastrophic and life-changing. He had undergone three surgeries so far, but had at least one more to go.

As someone who worked in the construction industry, the man said the incident had destroyed his livelihood, and he had to face the terrifying reality that he may never be physically fit enough to work again.

He also said that while the physical pain had been excruciating, the psychological trauma from the incident had been utterly devastating.

“I wish it never happened,” he said.

Deacon spent almost five months in custody before he was granted bail, then faced court again to be sentenced on Tuesday.

The court heard that a brick had been thrown at his car before he took his hands off the wheel.

His lawyer, Legal Aid’s Eliza Wilson, said it was his car that then veered before hitting the man, rather than him making his car veer at the man.

But she accepted nothing justified him removing his hands from the wheel before the crash.

Ms Wilson said Deacon started using drugs while young and had used illicit substances on the day of the offence. But since his arrest, he had completed a rehabilitation course and then got a job when he was released from custody.

The lawyer accepted her client’s actions warranted a term of imprisonment, but she argued that any time more than the five months he had already spent behind bars could be served as a suspended sentence.

“It’s fortunate there was no one else on the roads at this time, as there could have been a more serious result,” prosecutor Chamil Wanigaratne said.

Deacon pleaded guilty to causing grievous bodily harm, driving while suspended and driving an unregistered vehicle.

Magistrate James Lawton told him, “You could have so easily killed this man”.

But he said the steps Deacon had taken to rehabilitate himself were pleasing, and he hoped this would be “the line in the sand” that resulted in him becoming a law-abiding member of the community.

Deacon was convicted and sentenced to nine months’ jail, but the remaining four months were suspended for him to complete an 18-month good behaviour order.

canberra.title: Woman accused of firebombing home, threatening partner’s family
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged family violence. A young woman has been remanded in custody after she allegedly threatene...
canberra.content:
11 November 2026

A 25-year-old woman has been charged with arson over an alleged firebombing. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged family violence.

A young woman has been remanded in custody after she allegedly threatened her partner’s family, then firebombed a home in southern Canberra.

An ACT Policing spokesperson claimed the 25-year-old woman, who isn’t named to protect her alleged victims’ identities, sent a series of threatening messages to her partner and members of his family between Sunday and Tuesday (8 and 10 November).

In the messages, she allegedly threatened to injure them and damage homes and businesses connected with their family.

Police were then called to a home in Theodore late on Tuesday night.

“It is alleged the woman threw a homemade incendiary device at the residence, causing minor fire damage,” the police spokesperson said.

“During the incident, the woman also allegedly assaulted another woman known to her at the location.”

Officers arrested the woman at the scene and allegedly found a pocket knife, a lighter and a second incendiary device nearby.

The officers also allegedly found two more improvised incendiary devices in the woman’s vehicle.

The woman briefly faced the ACT Magistrates Court on Wednesday (11 November). She was charged with committing arson with the intent to endanger life, assault, possessing a knife without a reasonable excuse and using a carriage service to menace.

The duty lawyer, Legal Aid’s Niamh Dwyer, said her client would not apply for bail.

She said her client had no concerns for her own mental health and did not think she needed to be marked as a prisoner at risk when she was in custody.

But Magistrate Amy Begley said a mental health professional had recommended the woman be marked in this way, so she did so.

The woman, who sat in the dock glowering at the courtroom, was remanded in custody and will return to court on 30 November.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

australia.title: One Nation candidates say they are funding their own Victorian election campaigns as party keeps purse shut
australia.snippet: Exclusive : Party’s strategy questioned as campaigner says One Nation is not ‘capitalising on the groundswell’ Get our daily political em...
australia.content:
One Nation candidates in a number of winnable Victorian seats say they have been left to fund their own campaigns, with several questioning the party’s strategy ahead of the election.

Six candidates and campaigners, unauthorised to speak publicly, have told Guardian Australia their campaign material – including pamphlets, corflutes and roadside banners – have been paid for entirely through the $5,500 contribution they are required to make after being preselected.

They claim One Nation has not contributed any of its own money towards the material and that their payments will only be reimbursed if they secure at least 4% of first preference votes in their seat, which unlocks public funding for the party.

Two candidates have also said they were initially told their campaigns would receive a share of revenue from One Nation merchandise their teams sold. They claim that arrangement was changed in recent weeks, with all proceeds now going to the party.

The approach has left some within One Nation in Victoria concerned – particularly those with experience in other political parties.

One former Liberal campaigner, who is now volunteering for One Nation’s campaign in Melbourne’s outer suburbs, said the contrast between the two parties couldn’t be greater.

“In key seats, the Liberal party would be spending $100,000, if not more,” they said, requesting anonymity to speak without the party’s approval. “One Nation is asking its candidates to front up the cash and then submit an expense claim after the election.”

The campaigner said the One Nation candidate they were supporting was expected to pay thousands for their own election material – something a Liberal party candidate would “never be forced to do”.

They said One Nation’s approach was “really hard to understand” given the party could be entitled to more than $7m in public funding after the election, if current polling translated into votes.

“Why aren’t they spending the money?” they said. “They don’t seem to be capitalising on the groundswell of support they are receiving.”

Other candidates, including Michael Piastrino in the marginal seat of Berwick, have paid for additional campaign material after securing money from donors.

“If you can’t raise a couple of thousand dollars then don’t run as a candidate,” Piastrino said. “Anyone that wants to be a candidate needs to understand that you need to raise money. We are a fairly new party.”

Piastrino did not criticise the party for not spending its own money and said support for One Nation was already strong across the state.

During the federal election, One Nation asked candidates to sign an agreement outlining how they could submit claims for campaign expenses if they reached a certain vote threshold. Guardian Australia has previously reported on some candidates being left out of pocket.

Meanwhile, One Nation is spending less than the two major parties on digital advertising in Victoria. Analysis by the marketing and communications agency Populares shows the party has only spent $21,300 on Meta advertising since 1 September, compared with Labor at $2.81m and the Liberals just under $550,000.

“One Nation benefits overall from their organic content being favoured by the algorithm, but their candidates must be feeling left high and dry by the party when they see the advertising support their opponents receive,” said Populares chief executive Ed Coper, who previously worked with Climate 200 and some teal candidates during the 2025 federal election.

“Victorian Labor has spent as much as $80,000 on candidate-specific social media ads in some seats, whereas One Nation has only spent a quarter of that on their entire election campaign on paid social media ads.”

One Nation Victoria’s leader, Warren Pickering, has previously said the party was unlikely to run television ads and would limit doorknocking, something Labor considers one of the most effective ways to win over voters.

The former Liberal campaigner claimed One Nation was more focused on securing the balance of power in the upper house than building a strong campaign in lower house seats and suggested the party’s attention was instead on the New South Wales and federal elections.

In recent weeks, both Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce have played down the significance of the Victorian election as a measure of the party’s broader support.

Hanson told the Financial Review on Monday that while she expected pundits would be “shocked” at how well the party fares on 28 November, they were polling “far better” in NSW. Earlier this month Joyce described the Victorian election as “not a reflection of how One Nation is going nationally” in an interview with the Age.

One Nation did not respond to a request for comment.

australia.title: First Covid lockdowns, then alcohol to your door: rise in young Victorians with liver diseases prompts fears
australia.snippet: While young people are drinking less across the board, one expert says a small minority are actually drinking huge and damaging amounts o...
australia.content:
Rising numbers of young people are being hospitalised with severe, irreversible liver disease, as alcohol-related hospital admissions remain above pre-pandemic levels after peaking during Covid lockdowns.

A new Burnet Institute report, commissioned by the Foundation for Alcohol Research and Education (Fare), analysed nearly two decades of Victorian health data to examine the prevalence of alcohol-associated harm.

The study analysed 4,111 hospital admissions between 1 January 2017 to 30 June 2024, along with clinical data from 1 January 2010 to 30 June 2024.

When Covid lockdowns began in March 2020, treatment of alcohol-related hepatitis – a subset of liver disease – rose sharply, the data shows. They slowed after restrictions eased in late 2021.

But they have continued to be far above pre-pandemic levels.

The lead researcher, Prof Jessica Howell, said the rise correllated with a number of factors linked to the “overall stress” and “uncertainty” of lockdowns, although the report “can’t specifically tease out the causes”.

“Access to alcohol increased because you could get it delivered to your home,” she said. “So that really did lead to an escalation.”

While men made up the majority of cases, accounting for 62.5% of alcohol-linked hepatitis admissions, there was a “a sharp increase” among women.

Howell attributed the rise in excessive drinking to stress for women during Covid, “particularly on women who were primary caregivers, managing schooling, work and home.”

“A small proportion of women also were at home and at risk of being stuck in violent situations if they were enduring domestic violence. Lockdowns meant they couldn’t escape that.”

Rising numbers of young people affected

The data also revealed 14% of people admitted with alcohol-associated hepatitis statewide were aged under 35, and the report warned that a significant proportion of people with severe alcohol-related liver disease were under 40.

James O’Beirne, a professor of hepatology at Sunshine Coast university hospital and Griffith University, said he believed the trends could “undoubtedly” be identified in other states and territories with further research.

He has also noticed anecdotal evidence of such a trend in his work.

“Every week on the wards, we’ve got people under the age of 50 with very advanced liver disease and complications of cirrhosis.” O’Beirne said. “We’re seeing people being admitted in their 30s with severe liver disease.

“Women seem to be more susceptible to liver disease from alcohol than men because of their smaller body habitus.”

While the Burnet Institute’s findings appear to contradict other reports that show young people are drinking less overall, he said the previous research misses a key detail.

“While it’s true that younger people are drinking less alcohol across the board, there’s a subset of people who, unfortunately, are drinking a lot more. A small minority of young people are actually drinking huge amounts of alcohol.”

He said he also fears the changing drinking habits of young women “is leading to very advanced liver disease at an earlier age”.

“It’s well accepted that women are now drinking much more than they used to … there’s this concept of ‘wine o’clock’ that you see on social media, which I think is driving this normalisation of regular drinking,” he said.

Howell said the numbers “haven’t returned back to normal”, and fears they may not because “a new baseline of admissions for alcohol-associated hepatitis” has been set.

Fare’s chief executive, Ayla Chorley, said the report “brings to light that alcohol-related harm is very real”.

“Alcohol harm is on the streets, in front of nightclubs and pubs, and we’re now seeing it’s happening in the home,” she said.

Chorley said the findings highlighted the need for greater harm-reduction measures, including restrictions on alcohol availability, regulation and marketing.

“The alcohol industry has been very successful at individualising this condition, saying it’s an individual choice to drink responsibly … that discounts society’s expectations and cultural norms around alcohol consumption,” she said.

“People feel like: ‘Did I do something wrong? What is wrong with me? Why can’t I stop?’ And it is absolutely not on them. It is a harmful product. It is addictive by design and by its very nature.”

australia.title: ‘We were quite surprised’: Finland’s embassy goes viral with staff training day post on Instagram
australia.snippet: After a promotion for a ‘Finnish Dinner Date’ went ‘a bit viral’, the Canberra envoy’s next post became an unlikely social media hit Get ...
australia.content:
The embassy of Finland in Canberra was temporarily closed on Tuesday, 10 November.

Millions of people across the world were, it turns out, quite upset by this.

A day later, with the flourish of a ribbon-cutting ceremony, the embassy reopened its doors – having garnered many millions of views on its videos, spurred memes seen by millions more and social media attention across the globe, all unexpectedly from an innocuous Instagram post about a staff training day.

“We were all having a nice planning day, then someone said ‘oh my goodness it’s gone completely viral’,” Arto Haapea, Finland’s ambassador to Australia, told Guardian Australia.

The Finnish embassy, nestled in leafy Yarralumla in Canberra’s diplomatic zone just a stone’s throw from Parliament House, isn’t exactly a tourist hotspot in the nation’s capital. Flanked by the embassies of Estonia, Singapore, Mexico and Samoa, the sleek building – all grey panelling and glass – looks more like a bank or an office block than the genesis of a bizarre social media sensation stretching from Europe and the United States to the centre of Australian politics.

“The embassy of Finland in Canberra will be temporarily closed on Tuesday, 10 November 2026. Regular hours will resume on Wednesday, 11 November,” @FinlandInAustralia posted on Monday, with text over video of the northern lights glowing an eerie green.

Last week, the embassy’s other Instagram videos were getting like counts in the dozens or low hundreds. The post about the building’s opening hours has, as of time of writing, been liked 622,000 times, shared 405,000 times, and been seen by up to 10 million people worldwide.

How it got picked up by Instagram’s social media algorithm, and supercharged to be seen across the world, is likely something to do with the embassy’s previous video; Haapea promoting a competition to fly single people from around the world to Helsinki for a “Finnish Dinner Date”. The dinner date video also “went a bit viral”, Haapea said, getting 8m views and 163,000 likes.

“We were quite surprised by that,” the ambassador said.

Haapea said his team hadn’t had time to do any deep analysis of why these two clips went unexpectedly viral, but he theorised that the post with the opening hours “happened to ride on the same algorithm” as the dinner date, getting even more views, and attracting influencers, companies and brands around the world to make their own videos.

“POV you’re trying to enter the Embassy of Finland in Canberra but it’s 10th of November,” posted @j.ackdale, knocking on a locked door. That has 604,000 likes on Instagram at the time of writing.

“Me, all the way from Muscat, trying to get answers about the Finnish embassy in Canberra,” posted @sand_and_heels from Oman.

“I’m flying over 300 people from Finland to Australia. Hopefully the Embassy of Finland in Canberra is open today,” posted Finnish pilot @juusojelmer, to 88,000 likes.

That included Finnish politicians and ambassadors around the world, many of whom posted their own jokes, calling their colleagues or reassuring Finns in various countries that their embassies remained open. Haapea said even Finland’s foreign minister was keen to chat.

“We were done with the planning day and did a sauna with the team, and the foreign minister wanted to call about the planning day,” he said, as they filmed a video together – Haapea fresh from the sauna – promising that normal functions of the embassy would resume the next day.

On Wednesday, Canberrans from politicians to radio hosts and journalists visited the embassy, making their own social media clips live from the scene, while ordinary people tried knocking on the door or chatting to Finnish staff. A lighthearted video with a grand reopening, complete with ribbon-cutting ceremony, had to come next, Haapea said.

“We thank the international community for your fascinating interest,” the embassy posted.

As to why the interest in the first place? The ambassador said he’s still not sure.

“I think people are just looking for good news, to take their minds off all the craziness in the world. With the algorithm, and people who are good at making memes, all it took was a few big influencers to make a meme about it,” Haapea said.

australia.title: Anthony Albanese fails to mention fossil fuels in Cop summit speech
australia.snippet: Australian PM boasts of success in renewables but is criticised for not addressing the nation’s huge coal industry Get our breaking news ...
australia.content:
Anthony Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on climate change in a historic speech to the UN’s climate summit, but one which failed to mention the fossil fuels driving the crisis.

The Australia prime minister landed in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya on Wednesday morning where the Cop31 talks are being presided over by his climate change minister, Chris Bowen, but hosted by Turkey.

Only moments before Albanese spoke, on the same stage the UN secretary general Antonio Guterres said unambiguously that keeping the 1.5C temperature goal alive “means no new coal”.

In a packed conference room, Turkey put on an opening ceremony of whirling traditional dancers, booming music and a film shot around the world with characters saying “We need to talk”.

“This is an historic moment for my country,” said Albanese, adding Australia was “proud to be a leader on climate action.”

“Proud to be a renewable energy leader, creating the clean industries, businesses and jobs of the future. And proud to be here fighting for the interests of our Pacific family,” he said.

Australia had pushed for a role at the climate summit, he said, “because we wanted to speak for the people of the world who need urgent action, including those from our Pacific family”.

Australia is the world’s second largest exporter of coal for burning in power stations and the largest exporter of coal for steelmaking. A fifth of the world’s exported LNG comes from Australia.

Albanese pointed to “significant successes” for the country on climate change, including doubling renewable energy generation in six years that accounted for half of the country’s electricity, and building one of the world’s biggest rooftop solar and battery markets.

Guterres and several countries are pushing for the talks to progress a proposal from last year’s Cop hosts, Brazil, for countries to develop detailed plans to move away from fossil fuels.

Guterres told the conference: “Leaders – and in particular those from developed countries – cannot keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5 degrees.”

He said to keep the globally-agreed goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C within reach, coal power had to fall by at least 75% by 2035.

Unabated coal power – that is, coal generated without safely capturing the carbon dioxide emissions – “must be all but phased out” by 2040, and oil and gas use cut by a third, he said.

“Every government must align its policies, investments and infrastructure plans accordingly. That starts with credible national roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels — protecting workers and communities.

“That means no new coal. No new oil and gas infrastructure that puts 1.5 degrees further out of reach.”

Guterres and he has consistently called out fossil fuel production and lobbying and the lack of action on climate change as temperatures and weather extremes have worsened.

Adam Bandt, the former Greens leader and now chief executive of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said Albanese had “bluntly ignored” the secretary general’s message.

“The prime minister’s speech wasn’t just a missed opportunity, but by refusing to rein in coal and gas expansion or even mention it once, it was a snub to the secretary general’s call to tell the truth,” he said.

“At this summit, Australia is getting repeatedly called out for opening new coal and gas mines and the government can’t dodge it forever.”

Bill Hare, the Australian chief executive of Climate Analytics and a veteran of Cop meetings, said it was “disturbing” that Albanese had failed to mention fossil fuels.

As a major fossil fuel exporter, he said a “responsible leader” would have talked about developing a pathway out of fossil fuels.

“It still seems to be a dirty word. It’s the elephant in the room,” he said, pointing to 38 fossil projects approved by the Albanese government since it was elected in 2022.

Australia and Turkey are seeking support for a global goal to see 35% of final-use energy coming from electricity by 2035 – up from about a fifth today.

Speaking during a roll-call of heads of state and world leaders, Bowen said the world was asking if multilateralism could rise to a “polycrisis” of climate change, energy security, conflict and the power demands of artificial intelligence.

“Is international cooperation still a way forward? This fortnight we can answer those legitimate concerns and questions with a simple answer: Yes,” said Bowen.

australia.title: One Nation Victoria candidate apologises for slew of offensive comments about lesbians, Indians and Julia Gillard
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Chris Moore, running for the party in Greenvale, made derogatory social media comments between 2010 and 2012 Get our daily pol...
australia.content:
A One Nation candidate in Victoria has apologised for a series of offensive comments including repeated references to Australian-Indians as “curry munchers”, comparing a woman in burqa to a bag of rubbish, and sharing an image calling Julia Gillard a slut.

The party’s candidate for Greenvale on Melbourne’s north-western fringe, Chris Moore, also made derogatory comments about lesbians and refugees and once posted that he “doesn’t like the way the new homo cleaner at work looks at me”.

One Nation Victoria has not disendorsed the candidate over the comments, which were made on his personal Facebook page between 2010 and 2012.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

In a statement, Moore told Guardian Australia “these were unthoughtful posts I shared as a young man among close friends”.

“They don’t reflect who I am today,” Moore said. “Today I’m focused on doing the right thing by the voters of Greenvale, and giving them a strong voice in the Victorian Parliament.”

In 2012, Moore shared a picture of a woman and a child both wearing a burqa and standing between two full plastic rubbish bags. He then posted: “Haha spot the difference.”

Moore also shared an image of Gillard and the Home and Away character Alf Stewart. The image of Gillard was accompanied by the caption: “smash my box Alf!” The image of Stewart was accompanied with: “If I wanted a greasy red box I’d go to KFC ya slut.”

Moore also posted saying he “should probably stop shouting ‘Curry Muncher’ at the TV when I’ve got Indians living next door”. He also posted that he “wonders who does the dishes in a lesbian relationship?”

In 2010 he posted: “Just got the curry munchers to wash his car and pretty happy with the way it came up, looks like the boat people are good for something after all?”

Greenvale is a fairly safe Labor seat with a margin of 7.1%. It is held by Iwan Walters, a parliamentary secretary for multicultural affairs.

The electorate has a large Islamic and West Asian population. It has one of the highest proportions of people born in the Middle East and the lowest share of people with no religion.

At the last election, there was a swing of almost 15% against Labor on a two-party preferred basis.

A Liberal party campaign spokesperson said: “Mr Moore will be last on our how-to-vote card in Greenvale.”

A Labor spokesperson said the posts were “reprehensible” and called on One Nation to disendorse the candidate and for the Liberals not to preference him.

“There is no place for racist, Islamophobic and sexist comments,” the Labor spokesperson said.

On Tuesday, One Nation Victoria disendorsed its candidate for Preston, Franco Guardiani, whose private social media account described Adolf Hitler as the “GOAT” and claimed that “importing Islam is making pedophilia legal”.

The party’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, said Guardiani was disendorsed as soon as the comments were confirmed.

“At a time when Jewish Australians are experiencing unprecedented persecution, we are appalled that these comments have been made,” Pickering said.

Guardiani said he was disappointed by the party’s decision to dump him but understood their decision.

One Nation also disendorsed its candidate for the seat of Melbourne, Matthew Collins, over now-deleted comments on social media regarding a number of issues including sexual consent and pornographic jokes. Collins has apologised for the comments.

It is unclear how these candidate’s personal social media histories were not detected during candidate selection and vetting processes. The party has claimed to have invested time and money into improving this process.

In Victoria, One Nation candidates must provide their personal social media accounts for vetting. They are also interviewed by a three-person selection panel including Pickering and two party officials.

The Victorian Liberals also disendorsed the candidate for Williamstown, Paul Lindemann, after becoming aware of social media posts he had made that were offensive towards Indigenous people.

The party had been under pressure by Labor earlier on Wednesday to drop him after the Age revealed he received a six week suspension as a junior basketball coach after allegedly calling an under 14s player “crap”.

“This decision follows comments and views expressed by Mr Lindemann about Indigenous Australians that have recently come to light and were not previously known to the party,” a campaign spokesperson said.

“These comments are offensive, unacceptable and inconsistent with the values and standards expected of Liberal candidates.”

The posts, seen by Guardian Australia, were on an account named after Lindemann’s yacht and featured photos of him and his family. In them, he describes First Nations people as the “most primitive homosapiens on earth” and perpetuated racist tropes about “half-breed” and “full-blood” Indigenous Australians.

Losing Lindemann just weeks out from the 28 November poll is blow to the party, which had hopes of winning the western suburbs seat from Labor, despite it previously being considered a safe Labor seat.

A Labor spokesperson said: “Jess Wilson stood by Paul Lindemann when it came out he harassed and intimidated a girl at under 14s community basketball.

“These were disgusting and offensive posts and this individual should be expelled from the Liberal party.”

world.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
world.snippet: Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent Lewis Hamilton has visited Egyp...
world.content:
Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.

Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.

At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.

The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.

The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

world.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
world.snippet: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and...
world.content:
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.

The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment.

Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.

Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.

Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died, he said.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

Outside al-Wasta central hospital in Beni Suef province, where some of the injured were taken for treatment, survivors said passengers were in shock and struggling to breathe because of all the dust that was kicked up. Nearby villagers eventually got them out, they said.

Farha Gamal, a survivor who was inside the Fayyoum train, said she saw some of the passengers who appeared dead and others were struggling to find their way out of the car. “There were other cars that were completely mangled,” she said in an interview.

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the crash site to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002 when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

world.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
world.snippet: See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and...
world.content:
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.

See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.

The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.

“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”

Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”

See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

world.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
world.snippet: Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families The l...
world.content:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.

In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.

Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
world.snippet: Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result The African National Congress is on cou...
world.content:
The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.

Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.

The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.

The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.

Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.

The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.

In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.

With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.

Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.

Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.

The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.

With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.

Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.
